topic: Explain the Linux Boot Process: Firmware, Bootloader, Kernel, and Initialization
prompt: What are the four phases of the boot process on an x86-64 RHEL system, in order?
explanation: Firmware (BIOS/UEFI) runs POST and finds a boot device; the bootloader (GRUB2) loads the kernel; the kernel unpacks initramfs and switches to the real root; systemd then completes initialization by starting services to reach the boot target.

topic: Explain the Linux Boot Process: Firmware, Bootloader, Kernel, and Initialization
prompt: How is the 512-byte Master Boot Record laid out on a BIOS system?
options: 446-byte bootloader stub, 64-byte partition table, 2-byte boot signature
256 bytes each of bootloader and partition table
explanation: That 64-byte partition table is why MBR supports only four primary partitions. UEFI systems instead read a FAT-formatted EFI System Partition and can host multiple bootloaders.

topic: Explain the Linux Boot Process: Firmware, Bootloader, Kernel, and Initialization
prompt: What does the kernel do with initramfs during boot?
options: Unpacks it as a temporary root filesystem, then runs /init to prepare the real root before switching to it
Uses it as swap space until the real swap is activated
Copies it to /sysroot and leaves it there
explanation: /init is a minimal systemd environment that loads driver modules, activates storage, assembles LVM or encrypted volumes, then mounts the real root at /sysroot and performs a switch-root. initramfs is discarded from memory afterwards, and systemd starts as PID 1.

topic: Explain the Linux Boot Process: Firmware, Bootloader, Kernel, and Initialization
prompt: Which process runs as PID 1 after the switch-root?
explanation: systemd is the default initialization framework in RHEL 10. It starts the enabled userspace services and brings the system to its configured boot target.

topic: Interact with GRUB2 to Interrupt the Boot Process and Modify Boot Parameters
prompt: At the GRUB2 menu, which key edits the selected kernel entry, and which key combination boots the edited entry?
options: e to edit; Ctrl+x to boot
c to edit; Enter to boot
e to edit; Enter to boot
a to edit; Ctrl+b to boot
explanation: Press e to open the entry in a temporary editor and Ctrl+x to boot with your changes. Esc discards them. Pressing c instead opens the grub> command prompt.

topic: Interact with GRUB2 to Interrupt the Boot Process and Modify Boot Parameters
prompt: You edit a kernel entry at the GRUB2 menu and boot. What happens to that change?
options: It applies only to this boot; grub.cfg is not modified
It is written to grub.cfg and persists
It persists until the next kernel installation
explanation: Menu edits are one-time and temporary. To change boot settings persistently you edit /etc/default/grub and regenerate grub.cfg.

topic: Interact with GRUB2 to Interrupt the Boot Process and Modify Boot Parameters
prompt: Which line of a GRUB2 entry do you append a target name or kernel option to?
options: The line beginning with the keyword linux
The line beginning with set root
explanation: The linux line carries the kernel path and its command-line parameters. Appending rescue, emergency or 3 there boots into a less capable target.

topic: Manage GRUB2 Configuration to Persistently Change Boot Settings
prompt: Which file should you edit to change boot settings persistently, and which file must never be edited by hand?
explanation: grub.cfg is auto-generated from /etc/default/grub and the scripts in /etc/grub.d. It is rebuilt whenever a new kernel is installed, so manual edits to it are lost.

topic: Manage GRUB2 Configuration to Persistently Change Boot Settings
prompt: Regenerate the GRUB2 boot configuration file after editing /etc/default/grub.
explanation: grub2-mkconfig runs the scripts in /etc/grub.d in sort order, pulling variables from /etc/default/grub, and writes the result to the path given with -o.

topic: Manage GRUB2 Configuration to Persistently Change Boot Settings
prompt: Which directive in /etc/default/grub sets how long GRUB2 waits before booting the default entry?
explanation: GRUB_TIMEOUT defaults to 5 seconds. GRUB_DEFAULT chooses the entry (saved means the last one booted, 0 the first), and GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX supplies kernel command-line options.

topic: Manage GRUB2 Configuration to Persistently Change Boot Settings
prompt: Which statements about the /etc/grub.d scripts are correct? (Select all that apply.)
options: 40_custom is a template for custom menu entries
They are run alphabetically by grub2-install
explanation: The scripts are run in sort order by grub2-mkconfig, not grub2-install. Their combined output becomes grub.cfg.

topic: Manage GRUB2 Configuration to Persistently Change Boot Settings
prompt: What does GRUB_ENABLE_BLSCFG control?
options: Whether each kernel gets its own .conf file under /boot/loader/entries
Whether the boot menu is hidden
Whether legacy BIOS booting is allowed
Whether the boot log is written to disk
explanation: With the BootLoader Specification format enabled, entries live as separate files under /boot/loader/entries, named after the machine ID from /etc/machine-id plus the kernel version.

topic: Boot the System Into Specific Targets for Troubleshooting or Testing
prompt: Which strings can be appended to the linux line to boot into a less capable target? (Select all that apply.)
options: 1, s or single as legacy forms of rescue
explanation: Both rescue and emergency prompt for the root password at login. The legacy runlevel designations 1, s and single still map to the rescue target.

topic: Recover System Access by Resetting a Lost or Forgotten root Password
prompt: To reset a forgotten root password, what do you append to the linux line at the GRUB2 menu?
explanation: init=/bin/bash bypasses systemd entirely and drops you straight into a root shell, with / mounted read-only. rescue and emergency both demand the root password you do not have.

topic: Recover System Access by Resetting a Lost or Forgotten root Password
prompt: After booting with init=/bin/bash, the root filesystem is mounted read-only. Remount it read-write so passwd can update /etc/shadow.
explanation: Without the remount, passwd cannot write the new hash. Order within -o does not matter.

topic: Recover System Access by Resetting a Lost or Forgotten root Password
prompt: Why must you create /.autorelabel before rebooting after a root password reset?
options: To make SELinux relabel all files, including the newly written /etc/shadow
To rebuild the GRUB2 configuration on next boot
To force a filesystem consistency check
To clear the saved boot entry
explanation: Writing /etc/shadow from a shell outside the normal boot can leave it with a wrong SELinux context, which would break logins. The relabel restores policy compliance. Finish with `exec /sbin/init` to trigger it and reboot.

topic: Analyze the Linux Kernel, including its Package Composition, Version Anatomy, and Critical Directories
prompt: Display the version of the currently running kernel.
explanation: uname -r gives the kernel release, e.g. 6.12.0-55.9.1.el10_0.x86_64. Use uname -m to check the hardware architecture.

topic: Analyze the Linux Kernel, including its Package Composition, Version Anatomy, and Critical Directories
prompt: In the kernel version 6.12.0-55.9.1.el10_0.x86_64, what does 55.9.1 represent?
options: The Red Hat customised build of the upstream 6.12.0 kernel
explanation: 6.12.0 is the general upstream version (6 major, 12 major revision, 0 patch level), 55.9.1 is Red Hat's build, el10_0 names the Enterprise Linux release, and x86_64 the architecture.

topic: Analyze the Linux Kernel, including its Package Composition, Version Anatomy, and Critical Directories
prompt: Which files in /boot serve the described purpose? (Select all that apply.)
options: vmlinuz-6* is the compressed kernel executable
initramfs-6* is the initial RAM filesystem used in early boot
config-6* is the kernel build configuration
system.map-6* maps memory addresses to kernel symbols
explanation: /boot/grub2/grubenv stores persistent GRUB2 environment variables such as saved_entry — it is not versioned per kernel. symvers-6* holds symbol versioning for module compatibility.

topic: Analyze the Linux Kernel, including its Package Composition, Version Anatomy, and Critical Directories
prompt: Which directory holds the kernel modules for each installed kernel version?
explanation: Under /usr/lib/modules there is one subdirectory per installed kernel, named for its version. Its kernel/drivers subtree holds the hardware and software component modules.

topic: Update the Kernel by Downloading and Installing a New Version without Removing the Old One
prompt: What happens to the existing kernel when you install a new one with dnf?
options: It stays installed and remains selectable from the GRUB2 menu
It is replaced and its files are overwritten
It is removed once the new kernel boots successfully
It is kept only if you pass --keep-old
explanation: dnf adds a kernel rather than upgrading in place, so you can fall back if the new one misbehaves. grub.cfg is regenerated automatically and lists every bootable kernel.

topic: Analyze the Linux Kernel, including its Package Composition, Version Anatomy, and Critical Directories
prompt: Which kernel package contains no files itself but ensures the other kernel packages are installed correctly?
explanation: The kernel package is a meta-package. kernel-core has the essential modules, kernel-modules covers common hardware, kernel-modules-extra less common hardware, and kernel-headers the kernel-to-userspace interface files.
